He dismounted and tightened his girths, mounted again and dug in his spurs; and the horse leaped so powerfully over the gate that he came nowhere near it. Then Hermódr rode up to the hall, dismounted and went inside, and there he saw his brother Baldr sitting in the high seat; and Hermódr stayed there overnight. In the morning Hermódr begged Hel to let Baldr ride home with him, and told her how much weeping there was among the Æsir.

g-c49-21.s: But Hel said that this was how it should be tested whether Baldr was as loved by all as had been said: 'If all things in the world, living and dead, weep for him, then he shall go back to the Æsir; but he shall stay with Hel if anyone objects or will not weep.'

g-c49-22.s: Then Hermódr stood up, and Baldr led him out of the hall. Baldr took the ring Draupnir and sent it to Odin as a keepsake, and Nanna sent Frigg a linen smock and other gifts besides, and to Fulla a gold finger-ring.

"Then Hermódr rode back the way he had come, arrived in Ásgard and told everything he had seen and heard. After that the Æsir sent messengers all over the world to ask that Baldr be wept out of Hel. Everyone did so: people and living creatures, the earth, the stones, the trees and all metals, just as you must have seen that these things weep when they come out of the frost and into the warmth.

g-c49-23.s: When the messengers were on their way home, having carried out their errand well, they found a giantess sitting in a cave: she said her name was Thökk. They asked her to weep Baldr out of Hel; she answered:

l: Thökk will weep | dry tears
for Baldr's funeral pyre;
living or dead, | I had no love for the churl's son;
let Hel keep what she has!

g-c49-25.s: And people think that the giantess there was Loki Laufeyarson, who has done the most harm among the Æsir."

g-c50-1.s: Then Gangleri said: "Loki had certainly brought about a great deal, first by causing Baldr to be killed, and then by causing him not to be ransomed out of Hel. Was any vengeance taken on him for this?"

g-c50-2.s: Hárr answered: "He was repaid for it in such a way that he will remember it for a long time. When the gods had become as angry with him as might be expected, he ran away and hid on a certain mountain. There he built a house with four doors, so that he could see out of it in every direction. Often during the day he turned himself into a salmon and hid in the place called Fránangr-Falls; then he would wonder what kind of trick the gods might devise to catch him in the waterfall. As he sat in the house, he took linen twine and knotted it into meshes, the way a net has been made ever since; and a fire was burning in front of him.

g-c50-3.s: Then he saw that the Æsir were almost upon him; Odin had seen from Hlidskjálf where he was. He leaped up at once and out into the river, but threw the net into the fire.

"When the Æsir reached the house, the first to go in was the wisest of them all, who is called Kvasir. When he saw in the fire the white ash where the net had burned, he realised that this must be a device for catching fish, and told the Æsir so. They set to work at once and made themselves a net, copying the one they could see from the burnt-out ashes that Loki had made. When the net was ready, the Æsir went to the river and cast it into the waterfall. Thor held one end of the net and all the rest of the Æsir held the other, and they dragged it. But Loki darted ahead and lay down between two stones; they drew the net over him, and could tell that something living was in front of it. They went up to the waterfall a second time and cast the net, weighted with something so heavy that nothing could pass under it. Then Loki swam ahead of the net; but when he saw that it was only a short way to the sea, he jumped over the net-rope and made for the waterfall. This time the Æsir saw where he went. They went up to the waterfall again and split their company into two groups, while Thor waded down the middle of the river; and so they went out towards the sea. Now Loki saw that he had two choices: to dash out into the sea was deadly dangerous, and the other was to leap over the net again. That is what he did: he leaped as fast as he could over the net-rope. Thor snatched at him and caught hold of him, and he slipped through Thor's hand until the hand stopped at the tail; and that is why the salmon tapers towards the back.

g-c50-4.s: "Now Loki had been caught with no truce to protect him, and he was taken to a certain cave. There they took three flat stones, set them on edge and drilled a hole in each. Then Loki's sons were fetched, Váli and Nari or Narfi. The Æsir changed Váli into a wolf, and he tore his brother Narfi to pieces. The Æsir took Narfi's entrails and bound Loki with them over the three stones: one stands under his shoulders, the second under his loins, the third under the backs of his knees; and those bonds turned to iron. Then Skadi took a poisonous snake and fastened it above him, so that the venom would drip from the snake onto his face. But Sigyn, his wife, stands beside him and holds a basin under the drops of venom. When the basin is full she goes and pours the venom away, and meanwhile the venom drips onto his face. Then he jerks against it so violently that the whole earth shakes: you call that 'earthquakes'. There he lies in bonds until the Doom of the Gods."

g-c51-1.s: Then Gangleri said: "What is there to tell about the Doom of the Gods? I have never heard anything said of it before."

g-c51-2.s: Hárr answered: "There is great news to tell of it, and a great deal. The first is that a winter will come which is called the Awful Winter. Snow will drive from every direction; the frosts will be hard and the winds biting; the sun will do no good. Three such winters will follow one another with no summer in between. But before that there will be three other winters, during which there will be great battles all over the world. Brothers will kill each other out of greed, and no one will spare father or son in manslaughter and in incest. As it says in Völuspá:

l: Brothers will fight | and kill each other;
sisters' own children | will sin together;
evil days among men, | and much adultery:
an axe-age, a sword-age, | shields will be split;
a wind-age, a wolf-age, | before the world totters.

g-c51-4.s: Then something will happen that will be thought great news: the Wolf will swallow the sun, and people will think this a great disaster. Then the other wolf will seize the moon, and he too will do great damage; the stars will vanish from the sky. Then this also will come about: the whole earth and the cliffs will shake so hard that trees are torn out of the ground and the cliffs come crashing down; and all fetters and bonds will be snapped and torn apart. Then Fenrisúlfr will get loose. The sea will surge up over the land, because Midgardsormr is writhing in giant rage and making its way onto the shore. Then this too will happen: Naglfar will be set loose, the ship of that name. (It is made of dead men's nails; so it is worth a warning that if a man dies with his nails uncut, he adds a great deal of material to the ship Naglfar, which gods and men would wish to see finished as late as possible.) But in this flood Naglfar will float. Hrymr is the name of the giant who steers Naglfar. Fenrisúlfr will advance with his mouth gaping, his lower jaw against the earth and his upper jaw against the sky; he would gape wider still if there were room. Fire blazes from his eyes and nostrils. Midgardsormr will blow out so much venom that it spatters all the air and the water; he is truly terrible, and he will be on one side of the Wolf. In this uproar the sky will split apart, and the Sons of Múspell will ride out of it. Surtr will ride first, with burning fire both before and behind him. His sword is a very fine one: the light that shines from it is brighter than the sun. When they ride over Bifröst, the bridge will break, as was said before. The Sons of Múspell will go forward to the field called Vígrídr; Fenrisúlfr and Midgardsormr will come there too. Loki and Hrymr will also come there, and with Hrymr all the frost giants. All Hel's companions follow Loki. The Sons of Múspell will form a company by themselves, and it will be very bright. The field Vígrídr is a hundred leagues across in every direction.

g-c51-5.s: "When these things come to pass, Heimdallr will stand up and blow Gjallarhorn with all his might, and wake all the gods, and they will hold a council together. Then Odin will ride to Mímisbrunnr and ask Mímir's advice for himself and his army. Then the Ash of Yggdrasill will tremble, and nothing in heaven or on earth will be without fear. The Æsir will put on their armour, and so will all the Einherjar, and they will advance onto the field. Odin rides first, with his gold helmet, a fine coat of mail and his spear, which is called Gungnir. He will go against Fenrisúlfr, and Thor will advance at his side but will be unable to help him, because he will have his hands full fighting Midgardsormr. Freyr will fight Surtr, and it will be a hard struggle between them before Freyr falls: it will be his death that he does not have that good sword of his, which he gave to Skírnir. Then the dog Garmr, who is chained in front of Gnipa's Cave, will be loose: he is the greatest of monsters. He will do battle with Týr, and each will kill the other. Thor will kill Midgardsormr and walk nine paces away from the spot; then he will fall dead to the ground, because of the venom the Snake has blown on him. The Wolf will swallow Odin; that will be his end. But straight afterwards Vídarr will stride forward and set one foot on the Wolf's lower jaw. On that foot he wears the shoe for which the material has been gathered through all time. (It is the scraps of leather that people cut from their shoes at the toe or heel; so anyone who has it at heart to come to the help of the Æsir should throw those scraps away.) With one hand he will seize the Wolf's upper jaw and tear his throat apart; and that is the death of the Wolf. Loki will fight Heimdallr, and each will kill the other. Then straight away Surtr will fling fire over the earth and burn the whole world. As it says in Völuspá:

l: Heimdallr blows loudly, | the horn is raised high;
Odin speaks | with Mimir's head;
the towering Ash | of Yggdrasill trembles;
the old tree groans | when the giant breaks loose.
What of the Æsir? | What of the elves?
All Jötunheim echoes, | the Æsir are in council;
the dwarves are groaning | before their doors of stone,
those who know the rock walls; | do you know yet, or what?
Hrymr sails from the east, | the sea surges onward;
Jörmungandr | twists in mighty rage;
the Snake beats the waves, | the Eagle is screaming;
the golden-beaked one tears corpses, | Naglfar breaks loose.
From the east sails the ship; | Múspell's people are coming
over the waves of the sea, | and Loki steers;
there are the wizards, | all with the Wolf;
with them travels | the brother of Býleistr.
Surtr comes from the south | with the flame that devours branches;
from his sword shines | the sun of the gods of war;
the rocks are falling, | and the fiends stagger,
men tread the road to Hel, | heaven splits apart.
Then a second grief | comes to Hlín,
when Odin goes | to fight with the Wolf,
and Beli's slayer, | the bright god, against Surtr;
there Frigg's beloved | must fall.
Odin's son goes | to do battle with the Wolf:
Vídarr, hurrying | to meet the beast of slaughter;
with his hand he drives | the sword to the heart
of Hvedrungr's son; his father is avenged.
Now Hlödyn's | glorious son goes,
not fleeing from the Serpent, | heedless of fear;
all the children of earth | must leave their homesteads empty,
when Midgard's defender | strikes in fury.
The sun will grow dark, | the earth sinks into the sea,
the glittering stars | slip from the sky;
reeking smoke rages | and reddening fire:
the high heat licks | against heaven itself.
Vígrídr is the name of the field | where they will meet in battle,
Surtr and the beloved gods;
a hundred leagues | it measures on each side:
that field is fated for them."

g-c52-1.s: Then Gangleri said: "What will happen afterwards, when the whole world is burned, and all the gods are dead, and all the Einherjar and all mankind? Have you not said before that everyone will live in some world through all ages?"

g-c52-2.s: Then Thridi answered: "At that time there will be many good places to live, and many bad ones. The best place to be then will be Gimlé in Heaven. There is also plenty of good drink, for those who take pleasure in that, in the hall called Brimir, which stands in Ókólnir. There is another good hall which stands in Nidafjöll, made of red gold; its name is Sindri. In these halls good and pure-hearted people will live.

"On Nástrand there is a great and evil hall, and its doors face north. It is woven entirely of serpents' backs, like a house of wattle, and all the snakes' heads turn inwards and spit venom, so that rivers of venom run along the hall. Those who have broken oaths, and murderers, wade through those rivers, as it says here:

l: I know a hall that stands | far from the sun,
in Nástrand; its doors | face towards the north;
drops of venom fall | down through the roof-holes;
that hall is bordered | with the backs of serpents.
There are doomed to wade | the swirling streams
men who have sworn falsely, | and those who are murderers.

g-c52-5.s: But it is worst in Hvergelmir:

g-c52-6.s: There Nídhöggr | tears the corpses of dead men."

g-c53-1.s: Then Gangleri said: "Will any of the gods be alive then? Will there be any earth or heaven?"

g-c53-2.s: Hárr answered: "At that time the earth will rise out of the sea, and it will be green and beautiful; its crops will grow without being sown. Vídarr and Váli will be alive, since neither the sea nor Surtalogi will have harmed them, and they will live at Idavöllr, where Ásgard was before. Then the sons of Thor, Módi and Magni, will come there, and they will have Mjöllnir with them. After that Baldr and Hödr will come there from Hel. Then they will all sit down together and talk with one another, and call to mind their secret wisdom, and speak of the things that happened before: of Midgardsormr and of Fenrisúlfr. Then they will find in the grass the golden chess pieces that had belonged to the Æsir. As it is said:

l: In the shrines of the gods | Vídarr and Váli will live,
when Surtalogi has died down;
Módi and Magni | will have Mjöllnir
when Thor's fighting is over.

g-c53-4.s: In the place called Hoddmímisholt two human beings, called Líf and Lífthrasir, will lie hidden during Surtalogi, and for food they will have the morning dew. From these two will come so many descendants that the whole world will be peopled, as it says here:

l: Líf and Lífthrasir | will lie hidden
in Hoddmímisholt;
the morning dews | will be their food;
from them the generations are born.

g-c53-6.s: And it may seem strange to you that the sun will have borne a daughter no less beautiful than herself, and the daughter will then follow in her mother's footsteps, as it says here:

l: The Elf-beam | will bear a daughter
before Fenris drags her away;
that girl will go, | when the great gods die,
riding her mother's road.

g-c53-8.s: But now, if you are able to ask any further, I do not know where your answer will come from, for I have never heard anyone tell the course of the world at greater length. Now make what use you can of what you have heard."

g-c54-1.s: Then Gangleri heard great noises on every side of him; and when he had looked around him more, he found himself standing out of doors on a level plain, and he saw no hall there and no stronghold. Then he went on his way and came home to his kingdom, and told what he had seen and heard; and after him each person told these stories to the next.
[Here Wilken closes his edition; Jónsson admits the following:

g-c54-2.s: But the Æsir sat down to talk together, took counsel and recalled all these stories that had been told to him. And they gave the same names that were mentioned before to the people and places that were there, so that when long ages had passed, no one would doubt that the Æsir who were spoken of just now, and those to whom the same names were then given, were all one and the same. Thor was so named there, and he is the old Ása-Thor.

He is Öku-Thor, and to him are ascribed the mighty deeds that Hector performed in Troy. But people believe this: that the Turks told of Ulysses and called him Loki, for the Turks were his greatest enemies.]
